media_mentions.content: Abstract Mpox (formerly known as monkeypox) has re-emerged globally as a significant public health concern, with dermatology services occupying a key role in early recognition due to its predominant mucocutaneous manifestations. We present a series of four confirmed mpox cases diagnosed in April 2025 at a tertiary dermatology center in Jalisco, Mexico. All cases occurred in men who have sex with men, three of whom were living with HIV. Clinical presentations were heterogeneous, ranging from disseminated vesiculopustular eruptions with systemic symptoms to strictly localized, painful perianal lesions without prodrome. One case was initially misdiagnosed as herpes, underscoring the diagnostic complexity and potential overlap with other sexually transmitted dermatoses. Epidemiologic risk factors included recent unprotected sexual encounters and, in one case, recent travel. Diagnosis was confirmed by PCR and supported by compatible histopathology when performed. This cluster within a short timeframe reflects ongoing community transmission and highlights the importance of maintaining high clinical suspicion, integrating empathetic and stigma-free sexual history-taking, and leveraging epidemiologic clues for early detection. Increasing diagnostic awareness in dermatology practice is essential to mitigate under-recognition, guide timely management, and support containment strategies. Introduction Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is an emerging zoonotic infection caused by an orthopoxvirus, which has transitioned from a sporadic, endemic disease in Central and West Africa to a global public health concern since 2022 [1,2]. Although transmission historically involved animal-human contact, recent outbreaks have demonstrated sustained human-to-human transmission, particularly through close physical and sexual contact, with a disproportionately high incidence among men who have sex with men (MSM) [2-4]. The epidemiologic relevance of mpox has persisted beyond the initial 2022 multinational outbreak. According to World Health Organization surveillance, 63,692 laboratory-confirmed cases and 256 deaths were reported across 105 countries between January 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026 [5]. These data demonstrate continued global transmission and reinforce the importance of sustained clinical awareness even outside the initial outbreak period. Clinically, mpox is characterized by mucocutaneous lesions that classically progress from macules to vesicles and pustules; however, presentations are heterogeneous, and atypical forms confined to genital or perianal regions have been increasingly recognized [2,6]. Systemic manifestations such as fever, lymphadenopathy, and malaise may precede cutaneous findings but can be absent in a subset of patients, particularly those with localized disease [3]. Such variability may lead to diagnostic challenges and misclassification as other sexually associated dermatoses, including herpes simplex virus infection or syphilis, emphasizing the crucial role of dermatologists in timely recognition [2,3,6]. In Mexico, rising mpox cases have been documented intermittently since the 2022 global outbreak, with surveillance demonstrating ongoing transmission [4]. Early identification remains essential to limit spread and initiate adequate supportive care. Given the evolving epidemiologic patterns and potential under-recognition, dermatology services must maintain a high index of suspicion and integrate thorough, stigma-free sexual and travel history-taking into routine practice. This report describes four confirmed mpox cases diagnosed over a one-month period in a tertiary referral center in Jalisco, Mexico, highlighting clinical heterogeneity and reinforcing the importance of epidemiologic context in dermatologic assessment and early diagnosis. Case Presentation Case 1 A 41-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV presented with a one-month history of a disseminated polymorphous eruption including pustules, umbilicated vesicles, and crusted lesions on the face, trunk, extremities, palms, soles, and oral mucosa. Systemic symptoms included pruritus, fever, and cervical/inguinal lymphadenopathy. He reported multiple male sexual partners and recent unprotected intercourse. The eruption was initially misdiagnosed as herpes simplex infection, delaying appropriate treatment. Skin biopsy was compatible with mpox (Figure 1). Treatment He received symptomatic therapy with antipyretics, oral analgesics, antihistamines, and daily cleansing of lesions. Given his HIV status and extensive mucocutaneous involvement, tecovirimat was initiated. Response Within the first week, systemic symptoms improved and lesions began to crust. By day 18 of treatment, nearly all lesions had fully resolved. Follow-Up At four weeks, no new lesions were observed and all cutaneous and mucosal findings had healed without scarring or superinfection. His antiretroviral therapy was optimized after diagnosis. Case 2 A 40-year-old man living with HIV (treatment interruption three months prior) presented with localized painful umbilicated papules forming perianal plaques. Symptoms began one week prior, following prodromal fatigue and diarrhea. He reported more than 100 male sexual partners and recent high-risk anal contact. Biopsy showed findings consistent with mpox (Figure 2). Treatment Because of immunosuppression and severe perianal pain, he received nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), topical anesthetics, and hygiene measures. Tecovirimat was started due to clinical severity and uncontrolled HIV. Response He experienced significant reduction in pain and inflammation within the first week. Lesions crusted and resolved completely by days 14 to 16. Follow-Up At a three-week evaluation, all lesions had healed without functional impairment. He resumed antiretroviral therapy and was referred for sexual health counseling. Case 3 A 28-year-old man without known comorbidities presented with fever, headache, asthenia, and diaphoresis, followed by oral and pharyngeal lesions causing odynophagia. Days later, non-painful genital and hand lesions developed. He reported sexual contact with men ~15 days before onset and recent travel to Guanajuato. Skin biopsy confirmed mpox (Figure 3). Treatment He was managed with oral analgesics, hydration, and topical antiseptics. Due to severe odynophagia, topical lidocaine and short-course corticosteroids were used for symptom control. Antiviral therapy was not indicated as disease remained mild and he was immunocompetent. Response Systemic symptoms resolved within five days. Mucosal and cutaneous lesions crusted and detached over 10 to 14 days. Follow-Up At a four-week visit, no recurrence or complications were present. Only mild post-inflammatory erythema persisted. Case 4 A 32-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy and a recent history of tuberculosis presented with localized painful umbilicated papules forming perianal plaques, without fever or prodromal symptoms. Symptoms began abruptly two days after unprotected sexual contact. PCR and biopsy were consistent with mpox (Figure 4). Treatment He received analgesics, daily cleansing, and topical lidocaine for pain. Because of his HIV status and history of opportunistic infection, tecovirimat was started early. Response Pain improved markedly within 72 hours. Lesions showed rapid crusting and resolution during the following week, without bacterial superinfection. Follow-Up By the three-week follow-up visit, lesions had completely resolved with no scarring. His HIV parameters remained stable under ongoing antiretroviral therapy. Discussion This case series illustrates the evolving clinical spectrum of mpox and reinforces dermatology's critical role in early recognition and diagnosis. Since the 2022 global outbreak, mpox has demonstrated sustained transmission outside historically endemic regions, particularly among MSM [1,2]. Similar to international and national reports, the four cases in our series occurred exclusively in MSM, and three patients were living with HIV, a population shown to have higher incidence and occasionally more severe or atypical presentations [2,3,6]. Importantly, one patient in our series was immunocompetent, underscoring that mpox is not restricted to immunocompromised hosts. Compatible mucocutaneous manifestations may occur irrespective of HIV status, and epidemiologic exposure should therefore remain a central component of clinical suspicion [6]. Classically, mpox presents with a systemic prodrome followed by disseminated vesiculopustular lesions [2]. However, consistent with recent literature, our findings highlight significant clinical heterogeneity: two patients presented with isolated, painful perianal lesions, whereas one experienced initial mucosal involvement with odynophagia preceding the development of cutaneous findings. These atypical presentations align with recent evidence describing localized anogenital disease and mucosal-first involvement in sexually acquired mpox, which can mimic other sexually transmitted infections such as herpes simplex virus infection or syphilis [2,3,6]. One of our cases was initially misdiagnosed as herpes, underscoring how mpox can masquerade as other dermatoses, potentially delaying appropriate management and containment measures. Herpes simplex infection, syphilis, and other sexually transmitted infections were therefore considered clinically relevant differential diagnoses in this series. Importantly, the diagnosis of mpox was not established solely through exclusion of these entities but was confirmed by PCR, with supportive histopathologic findings when performed. A uniform laboratory screening panel for every alternative sexually transmitted infection was not consistently documented in the available clinical records. Consequently, these infections are presented as clinically relevant differential diagnoses rather than as uniformly laboratory-excluded conditions. Epidemiologic information remains essential for diagnosis. All patients reported recent sexual exposure, consistent with reports identifying close and sexual contact networks as important drivers of transmission [2-4]. Prompt PCR confirmation and histopathologic assessment when performed supported the diagnostic process. The identification of four confirmed cases within a single month at our center suggests ongoing regional transmission and potential under-recognition, consistent with continued surveillance reports in Mexico and internationally [4,5]. Vaccination represents an additional component of mpox prevention. Vaccines based on vaccinia virus, including Modified Vaccinia Ankara-Bavarian Nordic (MVA-BN) and LC16m8, are recommended by the World Health Organization for individuals at increased risk of exposure according to epidemiologic circumstances, individual risk, vaccine availability, and national public health policies [7]. Vaccine availability remains heterogeneous among countries. In the United States, JYNNEOS, an MVA-BN vaccine, is recommended for individuals at increased risk of mpox and may also be used for post-exposure prophylaxis when clinically indicated [8]. Although vaccination was not the focus of the present case series, awareness of available preventive strategies complements timely clinical recognition and public health containment. Our findings reinforce the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for mpox in patients presenting with vesiculopustular, mucosal, genital, or anogenital lesions, particularly when epidemiologic risk factors are present. Importantly, such suspicion should not depend exclusively on HIV status or the presence of systemic symptoms. A non-judgmental, detailed sexual history is indispensable for reducing missed diagnoses and stigma-related barriers to care [2,3]. Ongoing physician education and clear clinical protocols are necessary to ensure timely identification and mitigate further spread [2,4,6]. Several limitations should be acknowledged. This report represents a small retrospective case series from a single tertiary referral center. CD4 counts, HIV viral loads, specific antiretroviral regimens, and complete tecovirimat dosing and duration data were not consistently available in the clinical records. Likewise, laboratory testing for alternative sexually transmitted infections was not uniformly documented. Consequently, the present series was not designed to assess associations between immunologic status, specific antiretroviral or antiviral therapies, and disease severity. Nevertheless, these limitations do not affect the confirmed diagnosis of mpox in the reported cases or the primary descriptive objective of illustrating its heterogeneous dermatologic presentations. Conclusions This case series highlights the diverse clinical spectrum of mpox encountered in dermatologic practice, ranging from classic disseminated vesiculopustular disease to localized anogenital presentations with limited or absent systemic manifestations. The predominance of MSM and individuals living with HIV in this series is consistent with reported epidemiologic patterns; however, the occurrence of disease in an immunocompetent patient emphasizes that clinical suspicion should not depend exclusively on immune status. Early diagnosis relies on recognizing atypical forms, maintaining a broad differential diagnosis, and integrating thorough, stigma-free sexual and travel history-taking into routine assessment. Strengthening clinician awareness, ensuring timely access to diagnostic testing, and promoting preventive strategies, including vaccination when indicated and available, are important for avoiding misdiagnosis, enabling prompt management, and supporting public health containment efforts. Continued surveillance and reporting remain essential to better characterize evolving transmission patterns and the clinical behavior of mpox in diverse populations. title: Discrepancies between subjective and objective risk perceptions of monkeypox infection among MSM in China
abstract: The global resurgence of monkeypox presents a growing public health concern, particularly among men who have sex with men (MSM). Accurate risk perception is critical for effective prevention. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective risk perceptions of monkeypox infection remain insufficiently studied in China. A nationwide cross-sectional survey was conducted from 2023 to 2024 across 30 provinces. MSM were recruited through community-based organizations (CBOs) and voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) clinics. Participants completed an anonymous online questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, sexual behaviors, monkeypox knowledge, and both subjective and objective infection risk perceptions. Stratified logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with risk misperceptions. A total of 14,325 valid responses were analyzed. Of these, 46.66% (6,684) were high-risk MSM, and 71.78% (10,283) reported awareness of monkeypox-related knowledge. Among high-risk MSM, 11.70% (782) reported unexplained rashes or lesions mainly in the genital or perianal regions, while 4.22% (33) adopted no preventive measures despite potential exposure. Discrepancies in risk perception were observed, with 9.14% (611) underestimating and 22.31% (1,491) overestimating their infection risk, and 1.15% (9) showing severe mismatches between subjective and objective assessments. Younger age (18-25 years), residence in western regions, and offline partner-seeking behaviors were associated with risk underestimation, whereas higher education and online partner-seeking behaviors were associated with risk overestimation. Significant discrepancies existed between subjective and objective monkeypox infection risk perceptions among MSM in China, with overestimation more prevalent despite adequate knowledge levels. Tailored interventions addressing cognitive biases and behaviors are essential to enhance risk accuracy and prevention.

abstract_original: The global resurgence of monkeypox presents a growing public health concern, particularly among men who have sex with men (MSM). Accurate risk perception is critical for effective prevention. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective risk perceptions of monkeypox infection remain insufficiently studied in China. A nationwide cross-sectional survey was conducted from 2023 to 2024 across 30 provinces. MSM were recruited through community-based organizations (CBOs) and voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) clinics. Participants completed an anonymous online questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, sexual behaviors, monkeypox knowledge, and both subjective and objective infection risk perceptions. Stratified logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with risk misperceptions. A total of 14,325 valid responses were analyzed. Of these, 46.66% (6,684) were high-risk MSM, and 71.78% (10,283) reported awareness of monkeypox-related knowledge. Among high-risk MSM, 11.70% (782) reported unexplained rashes or lesions mainly in the genital or perianal regions, while 4.22% (33) adopted no preventive measures despite potential exposure. Discrepancies in risk perception were observed, with 9.14% (611) underestimating and 22.31% (1,491) overestimating their infection risk, and 1.15% (9) showing severe mismatches between subjective and objective assessments. Younger age (18-25 years), residence in western regions, and offline partner-seeking behaviors were associated with risk underestimation, whereas higher education and online partner-seeking behaviors were associated with risk overestimation. Significant discrepancies existed between subjective and objective monkeypox infection risk perceptions among MSM in China, with overestimation more prevalent despite adequate knowledge levels. Tailored interventions addressing cognitive biases and behaviors are essential to enhance risk accuracy and prevention.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated discrepancies between subjective and objective risk perceptions of monkeypox infection among men who have sex with men (MSM) in China. A nationwide cross-sectional survey from 2023 to 2024 collected data from 14,325 participants through community-based organizations and voluntary counseling clinics. The results showed that 46.66% of participants were high-risk, with 71.78% aware of monkeypox-related knowledge. elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者观察到风险感知存在显著差异,尽管知识水平较高,但风险高估更为普遍,这凸显了需要针对特定人群进行干预以提高风险准确性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为针对高风险MSM群体的认知偏差和行为进行定制干预措施提供了依据,以提高风险准确性并加强预防。

abstract_zh: 本研究强调了在检测和治疗传染病方面,机器学习(ML)相较于传统统计模型的日益增长的应用 [ 1 ]。CNNs 和 NLP 等机器学习方法用于皮肤病变和社交媒体分析 [ 2 ]。传统模型如回归和朴素贝叶斯用于疾病模式识别和病例预测。混合模型如 HMD 和 GRA-TLA 提高了预测准确性。本研究还讨论了挑战,并提出了基于提升的分类模型用于早期疾病检测和管理 [ 3 ]。

Volume 32, Supplement –Summer 2026 SUPPLEMENT ISSUE Supplement Monkeypox Virus Surveillance in Wastewater, North Carolina, USA, October 2023–May 2025 Cite This Article Citation for Media Abstract In September 2023, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services identified a new case of mpox clade II 5 months after the last previous report. To assess possible unrecognized transmission, nonvariola orthopoxvirus testing was implemented at select wastewater sites. During October 29, 2023–May 2025, a total of 801 samples were collected across 16 treatment plants serving ≈2 million residents. We analyzed wastewater detections (n = 47) and clinical cases (n = 45) using a +17-day window. Overall sensitivity of identifying the presence of >1 temporally aligned mpox case within a sewershed was 10.6% (95% CI 6.5%–16.7%); specificity was 95.1% (95% CI 93.2%–96.5%), positive predictive value was 31.9% (95% CI 20.4%–46.2%), and negative predictive value was 83.2% (95% CI 80.3%–85.7%). Restricting detections above the limit of detection reduced sensitivity but increased specificity. Overall, wastewater surveillance showed low sensitivity but provided complementary awareness for public health response. Since the first case was identified in a nonendemic region, mpox has emerged as an increasing public health concern in the United States. The global outbreak in 2022 affected 75 countries and territories; >2,300 cases had been confirmed in the United States by July 2022 (1). Because of evolving transmission dynamics, severity, and uncertainty surrounding social and economic impacts, the World Health Organization declared mpox a public health emergency of international concern on July 23, 2022 (2–3). Mpox is an infectious disease endemic to regions of Central and West Africa. It is caused by the enveloped DNA virus monkeypox virus (MPXV) and is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, lymphadenopathy, and a vesiculopustular rash that can involve the face, extremities, and genital region (3). Mpox is primarily transmitted through direct contact with active lesions, contaminated materials, bodily fluids, or respiratory transmission at close range (4,5). Mpox infections are categorized into 2 genetically distinct clades, clade I and clade II. Clade II infections, which were responsible for the global outbreak that began in 2022, are generally associated with less severe disease and reduced transmissibility (5). Historically, clade I mpox infections have demonstrated greater virulence, mortality, and transmission (6). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Wastewater Surveillance System initiated wastewater testing for MPXV in October 2022, five months after the mpox outbreak began in the United States. For underreported and stigmatized infections such as mpox, traditional case-based surveillance can present challenges, including incomplete capture of subclinical or unreported cases, making wastewater surveillance a valuable complementary approach to clinical mpox surveillance (5,6). Early work demonstrated that viral shedding through urine, feces, respiratory secretions, and skin lesions can result in detectable MPXV in wastewater, supporting wastewater-based epidemiology as a viable approach for monitoring and quantifying community transmission (2,7,8). In 1 study, MPXV detections in wastewater were shown to precede the identification of the clinical cases, highlighting its potential for early outbreak detection (9). Another study reported increases in wastewater viral concentrations ahead of reported clinical cases (5). Studies have also documented correlations between wastewater MPXV concentrations and incident mpox cases within corresponding sewersheds, supporting the utility of wastewater surveillance as a proxy for community-level transmission (10). Finally, wastewater detections in areas without corresponding clinical reports may help identify communities where mpox transmission might otherwise remain undetected because of social stigma, limited clinical recognition, or constrained diagnostic capacity (5,9). Recognizing wastewater surveillance as a valuable strategy for early identification of infectious disease activity, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services (NCDHHS) integrated mpox monitoring into its statewide wastewater surveillance program. In September 2023, nonvariola orthopoxvirus testing was implemented at selected wastewater surveillance sites across the state. That assay detects orthopoxviruses including vaccinia, cowpox, and all clades of MPXV. Primary sites were facilities in Asheville, Charlotte, Greensboro, Greenville, and Raleigh; additional periodic testing was conducted at selected sites in Cary, Chapel Hill, North Durham, and South Durham. To evaluate mpox wastewater surveillance program in North Carolina, we conducted this study to estimate sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) relative to confirmed clinical cases. Study Area and Surveillance Period We conducted a retrospective diagnostic performance analysis to evaluate wastewater surveillance for detecting MPXV circulation in North Carolina. For the period October 29, 2023–May 31, 2025, we compared wastewater detections from the North Carolina Wastewater Monitoring Network, operated by the NCDHHS, with confirmed clinical mpox cases using a +17-day temporal window. We assumed clinical case reporting to be complete for the purposes of this analysis. The study included data from 16 publicly owned wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) with defined catchment areas serving a combined population of 2,002,864 persons (Table 1). Facilities were in urban and semiurban regions and consisted of 4 plants in Charlotte, 3 plants each in Cary and Raleigh, and 1 plant each in Asheville, Chapel Hill, Greensboro, Greenville, North Durham, and South Durham. During the study period, 45 confirmed mpox cases occurred within the included sewersheds. We excluded sites sampled through CDC-contracted programs (Verily, https://verily.com) and WastewaterSCAN (https://www.wastewaterscan.org) because of differences in laboratory methods, assays, reporting structures, and sampling frequency. Clinical Case Data We also obtained clinical case data from NCDHHS. A confirmed mpox case was defined according to the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists case definition from 2022 (22-ID-10) as detection of nonvariola orthopoxvirus or MPXV DNA in a clinical specimen by PCR in a patient with compatible symptoms (11). We defined case date as date of symptom onset. We geocoded cases using residential address and spatially assigned them to sewersheds by using ArcGIS Pro (Esri, https://www.esri.com). Wastewater Sample Collection and Laboratory Testing. Influent wastewater was collected as 24-hour composite samples approximately 1 time/week at each WWTP except for the 3 plants in Cary and those in Chapel Hill, North Durham, and South Durham, which were only sampled selectively over the study period, generally in response to concerns about a confirmed or suspected mpox case in the general area. Samples were transported on ice and processed within 24 hours at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. We quantified MPXV DNA using the CDC Non-variola Orthopoxvirus Generic Real-Time PCR Test (12). We originally optimized the assay in a wastewater matrix by conducting a thermal gradient from 62°C–52°C to see which annealing temperature resulted in the greatest separation from positive and negative droplet clusters (Appendix Figure). We reported results as viral gene copies normalized to flow rate and population within the sewershed. We classified samples with concentrations above the assay limit of detection (LOD) as positive (n = 17). We experimentally determined the assay limit of blank (LOB) to be 0 copies/L by using methods adapted from Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute document EP17 (13). Because the LOB was 0, we theoretically estimated the assay LOD to be 500 copies/L, because Poisson distribution requires roughly 3 copies per sample to detect >1 copies with 95% probability (14,15). Using this strategy, we classified samples with concentrations from one half the LOD to the LOD as trace detections (n = 30). Overall Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, and NPV We classified wastewater observations as positive or negative on the basis of laboratory results, as described previously. For each wastewater sample, the presence of >1 confirmed clinical case within +17 days in the same sewershed was assessed. We selected a +17-day alignment window to approximate the biologically plausible period during which MPXV might be detectable in wastewater relative to a reported clinical case. Available data suggest that viral shedding is most likely to occur at 4 to 25 days (16,17) and might begin before diagnosis. Additional delays related to seeking care, laboratory confirmation, case reporting, and wastewater sampling can create temporal offsets between infection and detection. We selected the +17-day window to balance those biological and operational considerations while minimizing misclassification. We defined diagnostic categories as follows: true positive (TP), wastewater-positive and >1 clinical case within +17 days; false positive (FP), wastewater-positive and no clinical case within +17 days; true negative (TN), wastewater-negative and no clinical case within +17 days; and false negative (FN), wastewater-negative and >1 clinical case within +17 days. We calculated sensitivity (TP/[TP + FN]), specificity (TN/[TN + FP]), PPV (TP/[TP + FP]), and NPV (TN/[TN + FN]) overall and stratified results by WWTP/sewershed catchment. We calculated 95% CIs using Wilson score intervals because several sites had small denominators and proportions near 0 or 1. The primary analysis classified both positive and trace detections as wastewater-positive (n = 47). A secondary sensitivity analysis restricted wastewater-positive observations to samples exceeding the LOD (n = 17). Because clinical case surveillance is an imperfect reference standard and does not capture all infections, TP/FP/TN/FN classifications should be interpreted as concordance with reported cases rather than true infection status. All analyses were conducted in R version 4.2.3 (The R Project for Statistical Computing, https://www.r-project.org). During October 29, 2023–May 31, 2025, a total of 801 wastewater samples were collected across 16 WWTPs serving an estimated population of ≈2 million people. Of those, 47 (5.9%) were classified as wastewater-positive (17 above the LOD and 30 trace detections) and 754 (94.1%) were wastewater-negative. During the same period, 45 confirmed mpox cases were reported that fell within sewersheds representing the WWTPs in this study. Using a +17-day temporal alignment window, we classified 15 wastewater observations as TPs, 32 as FPs, 627 as TNs, and 127 as FNs (Table 2). The overall sensitivity of wastewater detection identifying the presence of >1 temporally aligned reported mpox case within a sewershed was 10.6% (95% CI 6.5%–16.7%). Specificity was 95.1% (95% CI 93.2%–96.5%). The PPV was 31.9% (95% CI 20.4%–46.2%), and the NPV was 83.2% (95% CI 80.3%–85.7%). At the WWTP sewershed level, sensitivity was highest at Charlotte WWTP 2 (25.0%) and ranged from 0% to 25.0% across sites with clinical activity (Table 3). Several sewersheds had no temporally aligned clinical cases during the surveillance period, resulting in undefined sensitivity estimates. Specificity was consistently high across sites, ranging from 71.4% to 100%. PPV varied widely by facility, ranging from <1% to 100%, reflecting differences in case occurrence and sampling frequency. NPV exceeded 69% at all sites with clinical activity and was 100% at several facilities without aligned cases. When restricting wastewater-positive observations to samples exceeding the LOD (n = 17), sensitivity decreased from 10.6% (95% CI 6.5%–16.7%) to 1.4% (95% CI 0.4%–5.0%), and specificity increased from 95.1% (95% CI 93.2%–96.5%) to 97.7% (95% CI 96.3%–98.6%) (Table 2). The number of FP observations decreased from 32 to 15, whereas FN observations increased from 127 to 140. PPV decreased from 31.9% (95% CI 20.4%–46.2%) to 11.8% (95% CI 3.3%–34.3%), and NPV was similar (83.2% vs. 82.1%). Site-level performance patterns were unchanged. This evaluation assessed the performance of wastewater surveillance for detecting MPXV across 16 WWTPs in North Carolina during October 2023–May 2025. Using a +17-day alignment window, wastewater detection demonstrated low sensitivity for identifying temporally aligned clinical cases (10.6% overall when including trace detections and 1.4% when restricted to detections above the LOD) but high specificity (>95%) and moderate NPV of ≈83%. We selected a +17-day window to account for the expected duration of MPXV shedding and potential delays between symptom onset, clinical diagnosis, and case reporting, while also accommodating once-weekly wastewater sampling. Because wastewater represents a composite, time-integrated signal and samples are collected weekly, this window reduces misclassification that could arise from temporal offsets between individual infections and wastewater detection. Those findings compare with national estimates reported in another study (16) that observed a daily sensitivity of 13.8% for detecting >1 person shedding MPXV and a weekly sensitivity of 31.7%. The lower sensitivity observed in North Carolina likely reflects differences in analytic approach, case density, and assumptions about viral shedding. Adams et al. (16) assumed complete case ascertainment and uniform 25-day viral shedding after symptom onset of mpox, whereas our analysis relied on confirmed case onset dates and a fixed +17-day temporal alignment window. This approach likely provides a more conservative estimate of sensitivity because wastewater detections occurring outside the defined window were classified as discordant even if they reflected prolonged or presymptomatic shedding. In addition, only 45 cases were identified across a population of >2 million persons, limiting the probability that wastewater concentrations would exceed detection thresholds. Despite low sensitivity for detecting single cases, specificity was high (95%–98%), indicating that wastewater-negative observations were generally concordant with the absence of reported cases. The NPV exceeded 80% overall and was higher at several individual sites, suggesting that the absence of a wastewater detection was associated with a low likelihood of concurrent reported cases. However, the PPV was modest (31.9% in the primary analysis and 11.8% in the LOD-only analysis), reflecting that some wastewater detections occurred without temporally aligned reported cases. Such detections could represent travel-associated cases, delayed reporting, prolonged shedding, asymptomatic or subclinical infections, or infections among persons residing outside the mapped catchment area. As a consequence, wastewater detections occurring without temporally aligned reported cases should not necessarily be interpreted as analytical FPs and might indicate true but unrecognized infections, suggesting that PPV might be underestimated. Therefore, if even a subset of those observations represented true infections, the PPV of wastewater surveillance would be higher than estimated in this analysis. Of note, sensitivity increased substantially when trace detections were included, indicating that low-level signals contributed meaningfully to temporal concordance with reported cases. That finding underscores the tradeoff between sensitivity and specificity when defining wastewater-positive thresholds. Restricting classification to concentrations above the assay LOD generally increased specificity but markedly reduced sensitivity, potentially limiting early warning capacity in low-incidence settings. In North Carolina, trace detections are interpreted within a structured public health decision framework rather than as definitive evidence of transmission and might prompt notification of local health departments and wastewater partners, review of recent case activity, enhanced syndromic surveillance monitoring, and coordination regarding case investigation or specimen retesting. Those actions are consistent with our public health action decision tree for confirmed detections (Figure). Confirmed detections might also involve escalation actions such as broader public notification, targeted outreach, and intensified sampling. Several factors likely contributed to the low sensitivity observed. First, mpox incidence during the study period was low and sporadic, reducing the probability that viral shedding might be detectable within large, pooled wastewater catchments. Second, sampling occurred once per week, which might have missed transient shedding signals. Third, wastewater represents an aggregate population-level signal, and the dilution effect within large catchments (some serving >500,000 persons) might limit detection of individual infections. Fourth, alignment relied on residential address assignment; persons infected but not residing within the sewershed would reduce measured concordance. The first limitation of this study is that reported clinical cases are not a perfect standard for infection. Our intent was to quantify the extent to which wastewater detections were temporally aligned with reported clinical cases within the same sewershed, rather than to provide an estimate of the true diagnostic accuracy of wastewater surveillance for detecting infection. analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the effectiveness of wastewater surveillance for detecting mpox virus in North Carolina, USA, from October 2023 to May 2025. A total of 801 samples were collected from 16 treatment plants serving 2 million residents. The CDC Non-variola Orthopoxvirus Generic Real-Time PCR Test was used to quantify MPXV DNA, with a theoretical limit of detection (LOD) of 500 copies/L. Overall, 17 samples were classified as positive, showing low sensitivity (10.6%) but high specificity (>95%). When restricted to concentrations above the LOD, sensitivity dropped to 1.4%, and specificity increased to 97.7%. The study highlights that wastewater-based detection can provide complementary awareness for public health response but may miss many cases due to low sensitivity. The findings suggest that trace detections contribute meaningfully to temporal concordance with reported cases, and the absence of wastewater detection is associated with a low likelihood of concurrent reported cases. However, the study notes that the positive predictive value (PPV) was modest, indicating that some wastewater detections may not align with reported cases and could represent true but unrecognized infections. The evidence is moderate due to the limitations of using clinical case surveillance as a reference standard.

Early work demonstrated that viral shedding through urine, feces, respiratory secretions, and skin lesions can result in detectable MPXV in wastewater, supporting wastewater-based epidemiology as a viable approach for monitoring and quantifying community transmission (2,7,8). In 1 study, MPXV detections in wastewater were shown to precede the identification of the clinical cases, highlighting its potential for early outbreak detection (9). Another study reported increases in wastewater viral concentrations ahead of reported clinical cases (5). To evaluate mpox wastewater surveillance program in North Carolina, we conducted this study to estimate sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) relative to confirmed clinical cases. Study Area and Surveillance Period We conducted a retrospective diagnostic performance analysis to evaluate wastewater surveillance for detecting MPXV circulation in North Carolina.
